case_info.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

[Case]
A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). case_info.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.

       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

case_info.explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Output STRICT JSON only:
{{
  "stage": "EXPAND | CHALLENGE | CONVERGE",
  "reason": "one short sentence: the hidden state you infer and why this stage now",
  "action_guidance": "concrete HOW-instruction for the AI's next utterance (no option letter/answer)"
}}

A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.
